content.text: CQRS

means using one model to change data and another to read it, where you'd otherwise use one for both. That's the whole pattern, and a read side that queries the same database still counts. Separate read stores, messaging and eventual consistency are optional next steps with real costs, and event sourcing is a different pattern that often travels with CQRS but isn't part of it.

The ticket said the order history page was slow. The design that came back was labeled "CQRS": an event store for orders, a message broker, a separate read database, and projectors to keep it in sync. It took a quarter to build. The page is fast now, and support has a new kind of ticket: "I cancelled my order and it still says Pending." The read database catches up moments later, but the customer has already taken a screenshot.
The common misconception
The belief: doing CQRS means event sourcing, a write database plus a read database, a message bus between them, and eventual consistency. Without those, it isn't really CQRS.

That picture didn't come from nowhere. The people who popularized CQRS also popularized event sourcing, and conference talks and sample apps usually show the two together. Most diagrams have two databases with arrows between them. Microsoft's Azure guide has sections on separate stores and on combining CQRS with event sourcing, and Greg Young himself notes that most query sides can be eventually consistent. Put together, the full stack looks like the definition.
The half-truth: those are things CQRS makes possible, not things it requires.
What actually happens
CQRS is one split: two models where there was one

Greg Young, who introduced the pattern, traces it to Bertrand Meyer's Command Query Separation: a method either changes state or returns data, never both. CQRS applies that idea at a larger scale: where one object handled both, you get two, one with the commands and one with the queries. In his CQRS Documents, a
CustomerService
becomes a
CustomerWriteService
and a
CustomerReadService
. Martin Fowler's description matches: separate models for update and display, which may share a database or use separate ones.
The read side can query the same database

Young calls it a thin read layer: it reads straight from the database and projects DTOs, bypassing the domain model. Microsoft's Azure guide calls separate models over a single data store the foundational level of CQRS, and the ordering service in Microsoft's eShopOnContainers reference app uses exactly that: one database, two logical models. In EF Core terms, commands load an entity, call its methods and save; queries project straight into DTOs with
Select
, which tracks nothing because the result contains no entities.
Separate stores are an optional, expensive step

A second store lets you shape and scale reads independently, with a denormalized view or a document database. It also has to be kept in sync, usually by publishing events from the write side. Azure's guide lists what comes with that: the database update and the event can't share a transaction, so it recommends a transactional outbox and idempotent consumers, and reads become subject to
eventual consistency
, so users may not see their own change right away. Young warns that synchronizing models can become very expensive.
Event sourcing is a different pattern
Event sourcing

changes how state is stored: an append-only list of events per entity, with the current state rebuilt by replaying them. An event store can only be read stream by stream, so event-sourced systems typically build separate read models, which is why the two patterns travel together. The dependency runs one way: event sourcing leans on CQRS, while CQRS works fine over ordinary tables. Microsoft is blunt about the cost: event sourcing is complex, costly to migrate to or from, and for most systems traditional data management is enough.
The fix: split the code, not the database

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: Both versions separate commands from queries, so both are CQRS. The first is wrong as a starting point: it pays for a broker, a projector and a second store before anything showed they were needed. The second does the split with the database you already have. The command side still enforces that shipped orders can't be cancelled, and the query side reads three columns without touching the domain model. In a test with EF Core 10 and SQLite, the list query selected only
Id
PlacedAt
and
Status
, the context tracked no entities afterwards, and a cancelled order showed as cancelled on the very next query.

rows.text: They're separate patterns; event sourcing leans on CQRS, not the other way round
CQRS needs a read database and a write database
The foundational form is two models over one database
Only when reads come from a separate store that's updated later
Azure's guide: messaging isn't a requirement for CQRS
CQRS belongs across the whole system
Fowler: use it on specific portions of a system, and cautiously

content.text: Once reads come from a separate store, every change is a database write plus a message, and they can't share one transaction. If the publish fails after
SaveChanges

, the read side never hears about the change. Azure's guide recommends the transactional outbox pattern and idempotent consumers, and you'll still need a UI that copes with users not seeing their own changes immediately.

blocks.title: Make the query side cheap first

content.text: Before adding a store, move reads to projections:
Select
into a DTO shaped for the screen, with no repository and no aggregate loading. If a screen is still slow, try an index or a database view next. Both keep reads consistent with writes.
How to apply it in your project
Put commands, which change state and return little, and queries, which return DTOs and change nothing, in separate classes. Sharing one
DbContext
is fine.

items.title: Keep the domain model on the command side

content.text: Entities and business rules live where state changes. Queries project with
Select
instead of loading aggregates with
Include
and mapping them.

items.title: Add a read store only for a measured need

content.text: Reach for a separate store when a query can't be made fast or scaled on the main database, and plan for the outbox, idempotent consumers and stale reads from day one.
Use it where history, audit or replay is a business requirement, and only for that part of the system, such as a payment ledger.
Key takeaways

items.text: CQRS is one split: a model for commands and a model for queries, where you'd otherwise have one.
A thin read side over the same database is the foundational form of CQRS, not a shortcut.
Separate read stores bring synchronization, an outbox and eventual consistency; add them for a measured need.
Event sourcing is a different pattern for storing state as events; it leans on CQRS, and CQRS doesn't need it.
Fowler's advice holds: apply CQRS to the parts of a system where reads and writes really differ, not everywhere.
